about: Transitions for SAT Reading & Writing (W2). logic_reasons[needed][picked] explains a wrong pick; {word} is the picked transition. also_reads lists logics in which a word can also read correctly, so it is never offered as a wrong option in a family of that logic.

logics.name: Contrast
logics.test: Does sentence 2 differ from or push against sentence 1?

logics.name: Concession
logics.test: Does sentence 2 hold even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grant a point against the claim?

logics.name: Cause and effect
logics.test: Is sentence 2 a result of, or a conclusion drawn from, sentence 1?

logics.name: Addition
logics.test: Does sentence 2 add another point in the same direction about the same subject?

logics.name: Example
logics.test: Is sentence 2 one specific case of sentence 1's general claim?

logics.name: Sequence
logics.test: Does sentence 2 only come next, earlier or at the same time, with no cause stated?

logics.name: Clarification and emphasis
logics.test: Does sentence 2 restate, sharpen or strengthen sentence 1?

logics.name: Similarity
logics.test: Does sentence 2 show a different case that works the same way?

logics.name: Conclusion
logics.test: Does sentence 2 sum up or judge everything that came before?

contrast.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1, but nothing in sentence 1 argues against it; the two sentences simply differ: that is contrast (“In contrast”, “However”).
contrast.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.example: “{word}” introduces a specific case of sentence 1's claim; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).
contrast.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 differs from or opposes sentence 1: that is contrast (“However”, “In contrast”).

concession.contrast: “{word}” only sets two ideas against each other; here sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).
concession.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 holds even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).
concession.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 holds even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).

concession.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 holds even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).
concession.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 holds even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).
concession.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 holds even though sentence 1 points the other way, or grants a point against the claim: that is concession (“Nevertheless”, “Admittedly”).

cause-effect.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.example: “{word}” introduces a specific case of sentence 1's claim; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.sequence: “{word}” only says sentence 2 comes later in time; here sentence 1 is the reason sentence 2 is so: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 follows from sentence 1 as its result: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).
cause-effect.conclusion: “{word}” sums up several points, but sentence 2 is the direct result of sentence 1: that is cause and effect (“Therefore”, “As a result”).

addition.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.example: “{word}” introduces an instance of sentence 1, but sentence 2 is a separate point, not a case of it: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.similarity: “{word}” compares two different cases, but sentence 2 adds another point about the same one: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).
addition.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 adds another point in the same direction: that is addition (“Moreover”, “In addition”).

example.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.addition: “{word}” adds a separate point; here sentence 2 is one instance of the general claim in sentence 1: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.clarification: “{word}” restates sentence 1 or makes it stronger; here sentence 2 moves from the general claim to one specific case: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).
example.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 is one specific case of sentence 1's general claim: that is example (“For example”, “For instance”).

sequence.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.cause-effect: “{word}” claims sentence 1 caused sentence 2, but the text gives no such link; sentence 2 is only the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.example: “{word}” introduces a specific case of sentence 1's claim; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).
sequence.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 is simply the next step in time: that is sequence (“Subsequently”, “Then”).

clarification.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.example: “{word}” introduces one case among many, but sentence 2 restates or sharpens sentence 1 itself: that is clarification (“In other words”, “That is”).
clarification.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).
clarification.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 restates or strengthens sentence 1: that is clarification (“In other words”, “In fact”).

similarity.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.cause-effect: “{word}” presents sentence 2 as a result of sentence 1; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.addition: “{word}” adds another point about the same case; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.example: “{word}” introduces a specific case of sentence 1's claim; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).
similarity.conclusion: “{word}” sums up the points before it; here sentence 2 turns to a different case that works the same way: that is similarity (“Similarly”, “Likewise”).

conclusion.contrast: “{word}” signals a contrast between the two sentences; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.concession: “{word}” says sentence 2 holds in spite of sentence 1; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.cause-effect: “{word}” treats sentence 2 as the result of the point just before it; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.addition: “{word}” adds another point of the same kind; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.example: “{word}” introduces a specific case of sentence 1's claim; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.sequence: “{word}” only places sentence 2 in time relative to sentence 1; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.clarification: “{word}” restates or strengthens sentence 1; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).
conclusion.similarity: “{word}” says sentence 2 is a different case that works like sentence 1; here sentence 2 sums up everything before it: that is conclusion (“In sum”, “Overall”).

entries.meaning: Signals that the next sentence differs from or goes against the one before it.
entries.short: signals a contrast or a turn
examples: Early astronomers assumed that comets drifted through Earth's upper air. [[However]], Tycho Brahe's measurements placed the comet of 1577 far beyond the Moon.
Most of the novel's chapters are narrated by the daughter. The final chapter, [[however]], is told from her mother's point of view.

lookalikes.tell: However only sets two ideas against each other; nevertheless says the second holds in spite of the first.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that differs sharply from what was just described.
entries.short: sets up a difference between two things
examples: Frogs of this species lay their eggs in standing water. [[In contrast]], the related salamanders bury their eggs in damp soil.
Northern factories relied on wage labor. [[In contrast]], the Southern economy depended on enslaved workers.

lookalikes.tell: In contrast compares two different things; nevertheless keeps one point standing despite another.

entries.meaning: Introduces a second thing that is being compared with the first and found to be different.
examples: The painter's early portraits use muted browns and grays. [[By contrast]], her late landscapes blaze with orange and violet.
Deep-ocean water barely changes temperature over a year. [[By contrast]], surface water can swing by several degrees.

lookalikes.tell: By contrast points to a difference; by the same token points to a sameness.

entries.meaning: Introduces the reverse case: the same relationship, but running the other way.
examples: When interest rates rise, borrowing tends to fall. [[Conversely]], when rates drop, households borrow more.
Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water. [[Conversely]], cold water can hold more.

lookalikes.tell: Conversely flips the relationship around; consequently gives the result of what came before.

entries.meaning: Introduces a second side or a different point of view, often weighed against the first.
examples: The new reading of the diary settles the question of its date. [[On the other hand]], it leaves the author's identity as uncertain as before.
Solar farms need large areas of open land. Rooftop panels, [[on the other hand]], use space that is already built on.

lookalikes.tell: On the other hand weighs a different side; in addition piles on one more point on the same side.

entries.meaning: Rejects the idea just denied and states that the opposite is true.
examples: The critic did not find the ending sentimental. [[On the contrary]], she praised its restraint.
The drought did not wipe out the lichen colonies. [[On the contrary]], several of them spread onto newly bare rock.

lookalikes.tell: On the contrary follows a denial and asserts its opposite; in contrast compares two different things.

entries.meaning: Introduces what happened or is true in place of the thing just ruled out.
examples: The committee did not adopt the proposal. [[Instead]], it asked for a smaller trial run.
The poet avoids naming her grief directly. [[Instead]], she describes the empty chair at the table.

lookalikes.tell: Instead replaces something that was ruled out; however just marks a contrast.

entries.meaning: Corrects the previous statement by giving the more accurate one in its place.
entries.short: more accurately, in place of that
examples: The fossil does not belong to an early bird. [[Rather]], it belongs to a small feathered dinosaur.
The treaty was not a victory for either side. [[Rather]], it was an exhausted compromise.

lookalikes.tell: Rather opening a sentence corrects what came before; rather than inside a sentence compares two options.

entries.meaning: Introduces a second thing measured against the first, usually to show how much they differ.
examples: The Amazon carries about a fifth of the world's river water to the sea. [[In comparison]], the Mississippi carries barely one percent.
The first printing of the novel sold eight hundred copies. [[In comparison]], the paperback edition sold two million.

lookalikes.tell: In comparison sets two things side by side to show a difference; in the same way says they match.

entries.meaning: Says that the next point is still true even though the previous one seems to work against it.
examples: The expedition's maps contained serious errors. [[Nevertheless]], they guided settlers across the plains for decades.
The drug caused mild headaches in some patients. [[Nevertheless]], most chose to continue the treatment.

lookalikes.tell: Nevertheless says the point survives the objection; however only marks a contrast.

entries.meaning: Says that something holds true despite what was just said.
examples: The sample size was small. [[Nonetheless]], the results matched those of much larger studies.
Critics dismissed the play as too long. It was [[nonetheless]] a success at the box office.

lookalikes.tell: Nonetheless means despite that; consequently means because of that.

entries.meaning: At the start of a sentence, says the next point holds even after what was just admitted.
examples: The theory could not explain every observation. [[Still]], it accounted for far more than its rivals.
The village had lost half its population. [[Still]], the weekly market went on.

lookalikes.tell: Still opening a sentence means even so; still inside it means continuing, as in still raining.

entries.meaning: Admits the truth of what came before but says the next point holds anyway.
examples: The factory's new filters removed most of the soot. [[Even so]], residents continued to report breathing problems.
The memoir leaves out whole years of the author's life. [[Even so]], historians rely on it heavily.

lookalikes.tell: Even so opens a new sentence after the admitted point; even though joins the admitted point inside one sentence.

entries.meaning: Introduces a point the writer grants, often a weakness in their own argument.
examples: The new vaccine is remarkably effective. [[Admittedly]], it must be stored at extremely low temperatures.
The biography is the best account of the senator's career. [[Admittedly]], it says little about his early years.

lookalikes.tell: Admittedly concedes a point against the claim; accordingly gives a fitting result.

entries.meaning: At the start of a sentence, concedes that a point is true before the writer's main claim.
examples: The survey reached only three hundred households. [[Granted]], that is a small sample for a city of this size.
The treaty's terms were harsh. [[Granted]], the defeated side had begun the war.

lookalikes.tell: Granted concedes a point; guaranteed promises that something will happen.

entries.meaning: Says that what follows happens or holds no matter what was just said.
examples: The forecast called for heavy rain on the day of the launch. [[Regardless]], the engineers kept to the schedule.
The painting's attribution remains disputed. [[Regardless]], it is among the museum's most visited works.

lookalikes.tell: Regardless is standard English; irregardless is a nonstandard form the SAT treats as an error.

entries.meaning: Accepts what was just said and then adds a limitation or a point in the other direction.
examples: The museum's new wing is striking to look at. [[That said]], its galleries are too dim for the paintings they hold.
The model predicts rainfall well in most regions. [[That said]], it performs poorly in mountainous areas.

lookalikes.tell: That said qualifies what came before; that is restates it more exactly.

entries.meaning: Says that something remains true in spite of what was just described.
examples: The expedition failed to reach the pole. [[All the same]], its maps of the coastline were used for a century.
The novelist disliked the film version of her book. [[All the same]], she attended its premiere.

lookalikes.tell: All the same means despite that; in the same way means similarly.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened or holds even though the previous point worked against it.
examples: The bridge's design was considered risky by many engineers. [[Despite this]], the city approved its construction.
The poet received almost no recognition during her lifetime. [[Despite this]], she wrote nearly two thousand poems.

lookalikes.tell: Despite this means the next point holds against the odds; because of this means it follows as a result.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that holds or happens even though the previous point pushed against it.
examples: Funding for the observatory was cut by half. [[In spite of this]], its staff catalogued more stars than ever before.
The strike lasted only three days. [[In spite of this]], it changed the city's labor laws.

lookalikes.tell: In spite of this means despite it; in light of this means because of it.

entries.meaning: Concedes a point, often before the writer turns back to the main claim.
examples: The reform did not end poverty in the region. [[To be sure]], it was never meant to do so on its own.
The composer's late symphonies are uneven. [[To be sure]], they contain some of his finest passages.

lookalikes.tell: To be sure concedes a point; to be precise sharpens a statement.

entries.meaning: Introduces a point that must be weighed against the one just made; it can also mean simultaneously.
examples: The law protected workers from the worst abuses. [[At the same time]], it made small workshops expensive to run.
The novel mocks the town's snobbery. [[At the same time]], it treats its characters with real affection.

lookalikes.tell: Simultaneously only means at the same moment; at the same time can also mean while that is true.

entries.meaning: Introduces a result or a conclusion that follows from what came before.
examples: The fossil lies beneath a layer of volcanic ash dated to 3.2 million years ago. It is [[therefore]] older than the eruption.
The letter mentions the fire of 1871. It [[therefore]] cannot have been written earlier.

lookalikes.tell: Therefore gives a result of the point before; furthermore adds another point.

entries.meaning: Introduces what follows as a result or a logical conclusion.
examples: The enzyme breaks down only one kind of sugar. [[Thus]], bacteria that lack it cannot feed on that sugar.
The council controlled the harbor and the roads. It [[thus]] controlled nearly all trade into the city.

lookalikes.tell: Thus opens a result or conclusion; thereby means by that means, inside a sentence, as in thereby reducing costs.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened because of what was just described.
examples: The river's course shifted several miles west. [[Consequently]], the old port town was left without access to the water.
The chemical breaks down quickly in sunlight. [[Consequently]], it rarely builds up in surface water.

lookalikes.tell: Consequently says one thing caused the next; subsequently only says it came later.

entries.meaning: Introduces an effect of what was just described.
examples: Wolves were reintroduced to the park in 1995. [[As a result]], elk stopped grazing along the riverbanks.
The printing press made books far cheaper to produce. [[As a result]], literacy spread rapidly across Europe.

lookalikes.tell: As a result names an effect of the previous point; in the end names a final outcome, however it came about.

entries.meaning: Introduces a result of what was just described.
examples: The glacier retreated rapidly after 1900. [[As a consequence]], the valley's streams now run dry by late summer.
The author's letters were burned after her death. [[As a consequence]], much of her private life remains unknown.

lookalikes.tell: As a consequence opens a sentence that gives a result; in consequence of names the cause.

entries.meaning: Introduces a conclusion or result drawn from what came before.
examples: The pigment appears only in paintings made after 1850. [[Hence]], the portrait cannot be the early work its owner claims.
Heat escapes more slowly through double-paned glass. [[Hence]], such windows lower heating costs.

lookalikes.tell: Hence means therefore; henceforth means from now on.

entries.meaning: Introduces an action or result that fits, or responds to, what was just described.
examples: Surveys showed that most riders traveled before dawn. [[Accordingly]], the transit agency added early-morning trains.
The soil at the site was highly acidic. [[Accordingly]], the farmers planted crops that tolerate acid.

lookalikes.tell: Accordingly means in response or as a result; according to means as stated by.

entries.meaning: Introduces what follows because of the reason just given.
examples: The manuscript is written in a code the author invented. [[For this reason]], scholars have been unable to read most of it.
Owls' feathers have soft, fringed edges that break up the flow of air. [[For this reason]], owls fly almost silently.

lookalikes.tell: For this reason gives a result of what came before; for example gives an instance of it.

entries.meaning: Introduces a result of what was just said.
examples: The island has no native mammals that hunt birds. [[Because of this]], several of its bird species lost the ability to fly.
The senator's speech was printed in every major newspaper. [[Because of this]], its phrases were soon repeated across the country.

lookalikes.tell: Because of this gives a result; despite this gives something that holds against the odds.

entries.meaning: Introduces what would happen if the condition just described were not met.
examples: The seeds must be kept completely dry. [[Otherwise]], they will rot before planting season.
Engineers had to reinforce the tower's base. [[Otherwise]], it would have continued to lean.

lookalikes.tell: Otherwise means if not; other than means except for.

entries.meaning: Adds a further point, usually one that strengthens the argument already being made.
examples: The new battery charges in under ten minutes. [[Moreover]], it holds its charge twice as long as older models.
The historian's account is well documented. [[Moreover]], it is supported by letters discovered after its publication.

lookalikes.tell: Moreover adds another point about the same subject; similarly shows that a different subject behaves alike.

entries.meaning: Adds another point in the same direction as the one before.
examples: The proposed dam would flood three villages. [[Furthermore]], it would block the river's salmon runs.
The novel's plot is gripping. [[Furthermore]], its descriptions of the city are exact enough to serve as a map.

lookalikes.tell: Furthermore adds a point; therefore draws a result from the point before.

entries.meaning: Adds another fact or point to those already given.
examples: The museum's collection includes over two thousand textiles. [[In addition]], it holds the region's largest archive of weavers' notebooks.
The treatment reduced swelling in most patients. [[In addition]], it shortened their recovery time.

lookalikes.tell: In addition opens a sentence that adds a point; in addition to joins two things inside one sentence.

entries.meaning: Adds another fact or point to the one before.
examples: The coral reef shelters hundreds of fish species. [[Additionally]], it protects the nearby coast from storm waves.
The reform lowered taxes on farmland. [[Additionally]], it abolished the tolls on rural roads.

lookalikes.tell: Additionally adds a point; accordingly gives a response or result.

entries.meaning: Adds a further point, often one that settles the matter.
examples: The committee rejected the plan as too expensive. [[Besides]], the site it proposed was already protected parkland.
The poet refused the invitation because she disliked travel. [[Besides]], she had a manuscript due that month.

lookalikes.tell: Besides means in addition; beside means next to.

entries.meaning: At the start of a sentence, adds another point in support of the argument.
examples: The study found that the plants grew faster in the treated soil. [[Further]], their roots were noticeably longer.
The law restricted who could vote. [[Further]], it made registration offices open only on weekdays.

lookalikes.tell: Further here adds a point; farther refers to physical distance.

entries.meaning: Adds a further point, often a stronger or more surprising one.
examples: The newly discovered frog is smaller than a fingernail. [[What's more]], it can change color in seconds.
The mayor's plan cut the city's debt in two years. [[What's more]], it did so without raising taxes.

lookalikes.tell: What's more opens a new sentence with an extra point; as well as joins two items inside one sentence.

entries.meaning: Introduces a specific case that shows the general point just made.
examples: Many desert plants store water in their tissues. [[For example]], a large saguaro cactus can hold more than a ton of water.
Several colonial newspapers mocked the new tax. [[For example]], one Boston paper printed its announcement inside a black mourning border.

lookalikes.tell: For example gives one case of a general claim; in fact strengthens or corrects the claim itself.

entries.meaning: Introduces one particular case of the general point just made.
examples: Some birds use tools to find food. [[For instance]], New Caledonian crows shape twigs into hooks to pull insects from bark.
The poet often borrows the rhythms of hymns. In "Night Watch," [[for instance]], each stanza follows a familiar church meter.

lookalikes.tell: For instance gives a case of the claim; in the first place gives the first reason in a list.

entries.meaning: Narrows a general statement down to the exact case or detail meant.
examples: The treaty changed the border in the north. [[Specifically]], it gave the river valley to the neighboring state.
The researchers tracked one change in the birds' behavior. [[Specifically]], they measured how early each morning the males began to sing.

lookalikes.tell: Specifically names the exact case meant; especially stresses one case above others.

entries.meaning: Singles out one especially important case of the general point just made.
examples: The novel's minor characters are vividly drawn. The landlady, [[in particular]], steals every scene she appears in.
Several industries depended on the canal. Coal mining, [[in particular]], could not have grown without it.

lookalikes.tell: In particular narrows to one case; in general widens to the usual pattern.

entries.meaning: Introduces an example chosen to make the general point clearer.
entries.short: to show this with an example
examples: Small changes in wording can shift how people answer a survey. [[To illustrate]], more respondents supported "aid to the poor" than "welfare," though the programs were identical.
The author builds suspense through delay. [[To illustrate]], the letter that explains everything is mentioned in chapter two but not opened until chapter twenty.

lookalikes.tell: To illustrate brings in an example; to clarify restates the point more plainly.

entries.meaning: Introduces the next step or event in order.
examples: The technicians first sealed the samples in glass tubes. [[Then]], they heated the tubes to 400 degrees.
Stanton read the declaration aloud to the convention. [[Then]], the delegates debated it paragraph by paragraph.

lookalikes.tell: Then refers to order in time; than is used in comparisons, as in taller than.

entries.meaning: Introduces the step or event that comes right after the one just described.
examples: The team first mapped the cave's entrance. [[Next]], they lowered sensors into the deepest shaft.
The printer set each page in lead type. [[Next]], he inked the type and pressed damp paper onto it.

lookalikes.tell: Next introduces the following step; finally introduces the last one.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened later, after the event just described.
examples: Tu Youyou isolated artemisinin from a traditional herbal remedy in 1972. [[Subsequently]], the compound became a standard treatment for malaria.
The poem first appeared in a small magazine. It was [[subsequently]] reprinted in newspapers across the country.

lookalikes.tell: Subsequently only says it came later; consequently says it was caused by what came before.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened after the event just described.
examples: The delegates signed the treaty in a small chapel. [[Afterward]], they walked together to the town square.
The divers photographed the wreck for three days. [[Afterward]], they mapped its position with sonar.

lookalikes.tell: Afterward means later; an afterword is a closing section of a book.

entries.meaning: Introduces what happened from that point on, after the event just described.
examples: The observatory opened in 1897. [[Thereafter]], it recorded the weather every hour for more than a century.
The author's first novel was rejected by nine publishers. [[Thereafter]], she published only under a pen name.

lookalikes.tell: Thereafter means after that in time; therefore means as a result.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened at a time after the event just described.
examples: The young botanist collected the plant on a riverbank in Peru. [[Later]], it was named in her honor.
The song was first performed at a small church gathering. [[Later]], it became an anthem of the civil rights movement.

lookalikes.tell: Later means afterward in time; latter means the second of two things named.

entries.meaning: Introduces what happened in the end, after a long time or a series of events.
entries.short: after a long time, in the end
examples: The seedlings struggled in the thin soil for years. [[Eventually]], they formed a dense forest.
The inventor's early engines kept breaking down. [[Eventually]], one ran for a full hour.

lookalikes.tell: Eventually marks when something happened, after a long while; ultimately can also mean at the most basic level.

entries.meaning: Introduces the last step in a process, the last event in a series, or the last point in a list.
examples: The crew poured the concrete and let it cure for a month. [[Finally]], they removed the wooden forms.
Negotiations dragged on through the winter. [[Finally]], in April, both sides agreed to the terms.

lookalikes.tell: Finally means last or at last; finely means in small pieces or with delicacy.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened before the event or time just described.
examples: The painting now hangs in the national gallery. [[Previously]], it had spent a century in a private collection.
Today the region grows mostly soybeans. [[Previously]], its farms had produced wheat.

lookalikes.tell: Previously means before; presently means now or soon.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happened before the event just described.
examples: The spacecraft reached Jupiter in 2016. [[Earlier]], it had swung past Earth to gain speed.
The novel ends with the heroine leaving the city. [[Earlier]], she had sworn she would never go.

lookalikes.tell: Earlier as a transition means before that; early means near the beginning of a period.

entries.meaning: Introduces something happening at the same time as the event just described, often somewhere else.
examples: Engineers spent the spring testing the rocket's engines. [[Meanwhile]], the astronauts trained in a desert far to the west.
The general waited outside the city for reinforcements. [[Meanwhile]], the defenders were quietly rebuilding the walls.

lookalikes.tell: Meanwhile means during the same time; afterward means after it.

entries.meaning: Introduces something that happens at exactly the same time as what was just described.
examples: The main telescope photographed the flare in visible light. [[Simultaneously]], a satellite recorded it in X-rays.
The two orchestras began playing on the same downbeat. [[Simultaneously]], the lights in the hall went dark.

lookalikes.tell: Simultaneously means at the same time; similarly means in a like way.

entries.meaning: Introduces what happens during the time before a later event.
examples: The new bridge will not open until next year. [[In the meantime]], a ferry carries commuters across the river.
The committee delayed its final vote until autumn. [[In the meantime]], members toured the proposed site.

lookalikes.tell: In the meantime means during the wait; in the end means when it is all over.

entries.meaning: Introduces what was true or happened at first, before a later change.
examples: The lichen now covers the entire rock face. [[Initially]], it grew only in the shaded cracks.
The composer's opera is now performed worldwide. [[Initially]], it closed after a single night.

lookalikes.tell: Initially means at first; initiative means the drive to begin things.

entries.meaning: Introduces a restatement that makes the previous idea more exact or easier to understand.
examples: The species is endemic to the island. [[That is]], it lives nowhere else on Earth.
The vote was unanimous. [[That is]], not one delegate objected.

lookalikes.tell: That is restates the point; that said qualifies it.

entries.meaning: Introduces a simpler or clearer way of saying what was just said.
examples: The treaty gave neither nation control of the strait. [[In other words]], the waterway remained open to all ships.
The infection was asymptomatic in nearly half of cases. [[In other words]], many infected people never felt sick.

lookalikes.tell: In other words says the same idea again; for example gives one case of it.

entries.meaning: Introduces a statement that strengthens, sharpens or corrects the one before it.
examples: The comet was bright enough to see without a telescope. [[In fact]], observers in Chile reported it in daylight.
Many readers assume the poem is about grief. [[In fact]], it was written for the poet's wedding.

lookalikes.tell: In fact strengthens or corrects the claim itself; for example offers one case of it.

entries.meaning: Confirms and strengthens the point just made, often with a stronger statement.
examples: The new reactor design was far safer than the old one. [[Indeed]], in ten years of testing it never once overheated.
The novelist was famous for her privacy. [[Indeed]], she refused every interview she was offered.

lookalikes.tell: Indeed confirms the point; instead replaces it with something else.

entries.meaning: Introduces the same idea expressed another way.
examples: The glacier loses more ice each summer than it gains each winter. [[Put differently]], it is shrinking year by year.
The court ruled that the law applied only to future contracts. [[Put differently]], existing agreements were untouched.

lookalikes.tell: Put differently restates the idea; differently alone just means in another way.

entries.meaning: Introduces what the situation amounts to in practice, whatever it is called.
entries.short: in practice, as it works out
examples: The law set a fine of one dollar for each violation. [[In effect]], it allowed factories to pollute freely.
The king kept his title but gave all decisions to the council. [[In effect]], the council ruled the country.

lookalikes.tell: In effect restates what the situation amounts to; as a result names a new effect that follows.

entries.meaning: Introduces the basic, central point of what was just described.
examples: The lengthy report recommends dozens of specific changes. [[In essence]], it asks the agency to publish its data.
The critic's review praises the actors, the sets and the music. [[In essence]], she calls the production a triumph.

lookalikes.tell: In essence names the core of one statement; in sum pulls together several points.

entries.meaning: Introduces a different case that works the same way as the one just described.
examples: Honeybees perform a dance that tells other bees where to find nectar. [[Similarly]], some ant species lay scent trails that lead nestmates to food.
Dickens published his novels in weekly installments. [[Similarly]], many of his rivals released their books chapter by chapter.

lookalikes.tell: Similarly means in a like way; simultaneously means at the same time.

entries.meaning: Says that the next case matches the one just described.
examples: The first colonists relied on the river for transport. [[Likewise]], the later mill owners built beside it to power their machines.
Tree rings record years of drought. [[Likewise]], layers of lake mud preserve a record of past rainfall.

lookalikes.tell: Likewise means similarly; likely means probably.

entries.meaning: Introduces a case that follows the same pattern as the one just described.
examples: A vaccine trains the immune system by showing it a harmless piece of a virus. [[In the same way]], fire drills prepare workers for a real emergency.
Chaucer's pilgrims each tell a tale on the road to Canterbury. [[In the same way]], the travelers in the modern novel take turns telling stories.

lookalikes.tell: In the same way means similarly; all the same means in spite of that.

entries.meaning: Introduces another case that works much like the one just described.
examples: Some lizards shed their tails to escape predators. [[In a similar way]], certain crabs can drop a claw when seized.
The early suffrage movement spread through local reading clubs. [[In a similar way]], the temperance movement grew through church groups.

lookalikes.tell: In a similar way compares two cases; in a sense qualifies how true a statement is.

entries.meaning: Says that the same reasoning that applies to the first case applies to the next one too.
examples: Regulators require that a new drug be tested for safety before it is sold. [[By the same token]], critics argue, a new pesticide should be tested before it is sprayed on crops.
A writer who takes bold risks will sometimes fail badly. [[By the same token]], a scientist who pursues unlikely ideas must expect many dead ends.

lookalikes.tell: By the same token applies the same reasoning to a new case; by contrast points to a difference.

entries.meaning: Introduces a brief statement that pulls together the points made before.
examples: The treatment lowered blood pressure, reduced hospital visits and cost less than the standard drug. [[In sum]], it outperformed the existing option on every measure.
The letters reveal the senator's doubts, his debts and his quarrels with party leaders. [[In sum]], they show a far more troubled man than his speeches suggest.

lookalikes.tell: In sum pulls the earlier points together; in addition adds one more.

entries.meaning: Introduces a short restatement of the main points.
entries.short: to sum up the main points
examples: The new trains are faster, quieter and cheaper to run than the old ones. [[In summary]], the upgrade has paid off.
The poems share a setting, a speaker and a set of recurring images. [[In summary]], they read as a single long work.

lookalikes.tell: In summary restates several main points; in short compresses one point into a brief statement.

entries.meaning: Introduces the closing statement of an argument or discussion.
examples: The data show rising temperatures, earlier springs and shrinking ice. [[In conclusion]], the region's climate is warming quickly.
The play's staging, casting and pacing all work against its script. [[In conclusion]], this production fails its source.

lookalikes.tell: In conclusion closes an argument; in consequence means as a result.

entries.meaning: Introduces a judgment about something taken as a whole, after its parts have been discussed.
examples: A few chapters of the history drag, and its maps are hard to read. [[Overall]], though, it is the best account of the war.
Rainfall rose in some provinces and fell in others. [[Overall]], the country received about the same amount as usual.

lookalikes.tell: Overall judges the whole; above all singles out the most important part.

entries.meaning: Introduces a brief summary of what was just explained at greater length.
examples: The bridge was over budget, two years late and closed for repairs within months. [[In short]], the project was a failure.
The novel's narrator lies about her age, her past and her motives. [[In short]], she cannot be trusted.

lookalikes.tell: In short means to put it briefly; shortly means soon.

entries.meaning: Introduces the final outcome or the final judgment after everything else is considered.
examples: The council debated the tower's design for three years. [[In the end]], it approved the original plan.
The heroine weighs duty against love for most of the novel. [[In the end]], she chooses neither.

lookalikes.tell: In the end means when it is all over; in the meantime means while waiting.

entries.meaning: Introduces an overall judgment after the details have been weighed.
examples: The festival was crowded and one stage lost power. [[All in all]], organizers called it their most successful year.
The experiment had some setbacks, but most of its predictions held. [[All in all]], the team considered it a success.

lookalikes.tell: All in all sums up; all the same means in spite of that.

entries.meaning: Introduces the final result or the most basic point, after everything else is considered.
examples: The two nations negotiated over the border for a decade. [[Ultimately]], they agreed to let an international court decide.
The essay discusses style, structure and sources. [[Ultimately]], though, its argument rests on a single letter.

lookalikes.tell: Ultimately can mean at the most basic level; eventually only means after a long time.

entries.meaning: Introduces a general judgment that holds for most of what was described, despite exceptions.
examples: Some of the colony's settlers suffered through the first winters. [[On the whole]], the colony prospered.
Critics disagreed about the director's choices in several scenes. [[On the whole]], they praised the film.

lookalikes.tell: On the whole sums up the general picture; on the other hand introduces the other side.

entries.meaning: Introduces a short summary of the points just made.
examples: The site has fresh water, good soil and a natural harbor. [[To sum up]], it was an ideal place for a settlement.
The poet cuts every extra word, avoids rhyme and ends lines mid-thought. [[To sum up]], her style is spare and restless.

lookalikes.tell: To sum up summarizes the points; to some extent limits how far a claim holds.
